Counts German bottle deposits.

A barcode does not carry its deposit — single-use containers are marked with the DPG security label, not in the number. So this app ships a list of what can be decided (cans are single-use by law, 0,25€) and learns the rest from you: asked once, remembered for good.

%1$d barcodes shipped, %2$d learned by you.

Product names and packaging data: Open Food Facts, Open Beauty Facts and Open Products Facts, used under the Open Database License (ODbL). Barcode reading: ZXing (Apache 2.0).

A small logo of a bottle and a can with a curved arrow (DPG)
Or a reusable-bottle logo — typical for water or soft drinks from a crate
No deposit logo and no “Mehrweg” anywhere
All %1$d products of this maker in the list carry %2$s. A guess from the maker number in the barcode, right about 9 times in 10 when tested. Check the bottle.
Open Food Facts lists it as yogurt or cream in glass marked “Mehrweg” or “Pfand”. Such jars usually carry 0,15€.

Many jars are single-use, some yogurts too
Reusable jars for yogurt, cream and quark usually carry 0,15€ — many dairies share the same reusable jar.
A jar without a reusable mark is single-use and carries no deposit. It goes into the bottle bank.

Every drink can from 0.1 to 3 litres carries 0,25€ by law — whatever is inside.
Cartons and pouches carry no deposit by law. Put it in the recycling bin.
This logo marks every single-use bottle with deposit. By law it is 0,25€ — whatever is inside, juice and milk included.
Reusable plastic bottles go back to the bottler and are refilled. They usually carry 0,15€.
Single-use bottles with deposit must be marked. No mark usually means it was not sold with German deposit — often an import. The machine will likely refuse it.
Swing-top bottles are reusable and usually carry 0,15€.
Standard beer bottles from the shared German pool carry 0,08€.
Reusable glass for water, juice and soft drinks usually carries 0,15€.
A single-use glass bottle of beer, water or soft drink carries 0,25€ by law, like a can.
Wine, sparkling wine, spirits, and juice in single-use glass carry no deposit by law. Glass goes into the bottle bank.
Deposit on reusable bottles and jars is set by the bottler, not by law. 0,08€ and 0,15€ are the usual amounts; the app remembers what you choose, and you can change it later.

Tap “Ask Jev” on an unknown drink to send it to Jev (jev-1.13 by TypeSafe) for a deposit suggestion — through OpenRouter or directly at TypeSafe, whichever key you give. What goes out: the product name, size, packaging and category from Open Food Facts — not the barcode, nothing about you. Jev only suggests; you still tap the answer.

Each question costs a fraction of a cent on that account. Asked so far on this phone: %1$d, cost %2$s.

Each key stays on this phone, is left out of backups and is never shown again. Tip: make a separate key with a spending limit.
Directly at TypeSafe (key from typesafe.ai, not tested yet)
No key set — Jev is off.
Key saved. Tap “Ask Jev” on the next unknown barcode to use it.
Key removed. Jev keeps asking the other way.
Point the camera at the barcode. Known drinks are counted at once, with their deposit.
The app asks once how much deposit is on it and remembers your answer for good.
Count by hand with +0,08€, +0,15€, +0,25€ and +Crate. “Not sure?” asks a few questions about the bottle and tells you its deposit.
Tap a line to change it, use − and + for the number. “Reset” clears the list; tap it again to get it back. “Share” sends the count as text.
For a drink the app does not know, “Ask Jev” suggests a deposit and shows how sure it is. You still decide.

Only the product name, size, packaging and category. No barcode, nothing about you, and only when you tap. You need your own key from OpenRouter or TypeSafe; each question costs a fraction of a cent. Jev is off until you switch it on under Settings › Jev suggestions.
Names come from Open Food Facts: to look one up, the app sends the barcode there. Your list and your answers stay on your phone.
By law every single-use bottle and can carries 0,25€. Reusable bottles usually carry 0,08€ (beer) or 0,15€.

Plastic bottles, cans and single-use glass bottles from 0.1 to 3 litres carry 0,25€ by law. They are marked, usually with the deposit logo (a bottle and a can with a curved arrow) next to the barcode.
Glass beer bottles up to 0.5 l from the shared pool, with a crown cap.
Water, juice and soft drinks in reusable glass or plastic, swing-top bottles and many yogurt jars. Look for the word “Mehrweg”. The bottler sets these amounts, not the law.
A crate has its own deposit on top of the bottles in it, often 1,50€. The bottler sets it.
Cartons and drink pouches; wine, sparkling wine and spirits; milk, juice and nectar in glass or cartons; drinks for babies. But in a plastic bottle or a can, milk and juice carry 0,25€ too.

Any shop that sells single-use drinks in the same material (plastic, glass or cans) must take them back, wherever you bought them. Shops smaller than 200 m² only take back the brands they sell. Reusable bottles go back to shops that sell them.
The machine prints a receipt; you get the money at the checkout or take it off your shopping. It stays valid for years, so there is no rush.
Law: § 46 VerpackDG. Only the 0,25€ for single-use is set by law.

Pfand Counter helps you estimate your deposit, but it can be wrong. A barcode does not carry its deposit, so the list, the guesses and Jev\'s suggestions can make mistakes. What counts is what the machine or the shop pays out. Check unusual bottles yourself.
I understand that the app can make mistakes
Written with AI by a layperson, not reviewed by an expert.
%1$s — a crate with its own barcode
%1$s — half of a crate that splits in two
The crate and all its bottles with one tap.
Does the crate have its own barcode? Scan it and choose “crate” — the app remembers it.
Please fill in a name, 1 to 60 bottles and an amount.
A crate carries no mark that tells its deposit. The bottler sets it; most crates carry 1,50€.
Can the crate be pulled apart into two halves?
The usual crate for beer, water or juice
Crates usually carry 1,50€ of their own, on top of the bottles in them.
Each half of such a crate gives back half the deposit; the whole crate gives 1,50€.
If the machine or the shop pays another amount, choose “Other amount” and type it in.
Some crates hold single-use plastic bottles, often with the PET-Cycle mark. They carry 0,25€ each: choose 0,25€ under “Deposit per bottle”.
The shop must still take the crate back. It may only keep the deposit of the broken bottle.
Sources: Wikipedia “Getränkekiste”; consumer advice centre, “Mehrweg oder Einweg”.

Opens your map app. Shops that sell single-use drinks with deposit must take back empty ones of the same material (plastic, glass or can), wherever you bought them. Shops under 200 m² only take back the brands they sell.
Off unless you switch them on here, also with a screen reader, so they do not talk over it. The phone vibrates either way.
No map app found. Install one to search for shops nearby.
No account, no ads, no tracking and no server of its own. Your count stays on your phone. Only the scanned barcode goes to the open database Open Food Facts, to show the product name.
The camera only reads barcodes. The images are checked in the phone\'s memory; no photo is saved or sent.

To find a product name, the app sends the barcode, an app name and, as with any internet request, your IP address to Open Food Facts, a non-profit association in France. If it does not know the product, the same goes to its sister databases Open Beauty Facts and Open Products Facts. Their privacy policy: https://world.openfoodfacts.org/privacy

Only if you switched Jev on in Settings, entered your own key for OpenRouter or TypeSafe and tap “Ask Jev”. The chosen provider then gets a product description (name, size, packaging, up to three categories), your key and your IP address, but not the barcode. Their privacy policies: https://openrouter.ai/privacy and https://typesafe.ai/legal/privacy-policy

“Share” hands your count as text to the app you pick. “Supermarket nearby” hands the word “supermarket” to your map app; what it does with your location is up to that app. “Report a translation mistake” opens a GitHub page in your browser; nothing is sent until you send it there.

In the app\'s private storage, which other apps cannot read: your list and one step for undo, the barcodes you taught, crate deposit and crate sizes, your settings, the statistics page and, if entered, your Jev key and question counter. The key is left out of Android backups; the rest may be backed up if you turned backups on. Uninstalling the app or clearing its data deletes everything.
What the app does not do

No ads, no analytics, no crash reports. The statistics page is only for you and never leaves the phone. No account, no location, no contacts, no photos or files. Permissions: camera, internet, vibration.

The developer receives no data from the app, so there is nothing to disclose or delete. You delete the data on your phone yourself; for data at Open Food Facts or the AI provider, contact them. You may complain to a data protection authority.
